item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I thought this had an excellent start. I liked the sense of wonder and mystery from the perspective of the girl, which unfortunately was sabotaged by the second half of the story, mostly due to the abrupt change in tone and the ending.

I think I might have preferred the story being told entirely from the perspective of our universe, and letting the Foundation intervention and accompanying pathos occur through that lens.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I really wish you would have explored more about how Jane ran into the Foundation. It might have helped some of the ending seem less… abrupt. I know I told you when we reviewed this draft that you needed to tighten your belt a bit, and It seems you took some of that advice, but the ending here, with the brain tumor, comes out of absolutely nowhere.

I would have preferred her to run headlong into that foolish quest to find her friend than to suddenly get cancer and die… If my advice led you down this path, I'm sorry. But I just don't like how this ended up.

-1

item.content:encoded:
I very much liked the SCP you used for this, and the relationship of young girl and an old woman shared between two worlds was very much a smile maker, but I was a bit disappointed by the ending.

I thought the two fishermen inviting Gedril out knew about her connections to the other world and were gonna snatch her, or Gedril was going to act out against the Foundation agents at the other end by doing something drastic. But instead, she died from a tumor. I felt like a lot more could have been done here but wasn't. (Possibly due to a deadline? Because that's understandable.)

In the end, it started out great but ended with a let down. I think I'm going to leave this as a neutral vote.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I don't like this for a couple of reasons.

Mechanically, it's kind of shoddy. The punctuation for the quotations is off—it should look like this: "I'm being pedantic," said Chubert, instead of "I'm being pedantic." said Chubert. There are a ton of tense issues in which you mix past and present tense.

I'm kind of irked by the world-building, which doesn't hold any consistency—it just seems to be quirky and whimsical for the sake of being quirky and whimsical, which I suppose is a fault of the article itself. Emotionally speaking, there isn't any opportunity for me to actually experience any emotion, because it's just flat out getting shoved down my face, "this person is sad." Cliche criticism, but still valid: show, don't tell.

I find the plot really trite and saccharine. Like, the last section is just so cliche and cheesy. "Life is short, you have to live it all!" Then she signs up for a charity? After she gets a brain tumor? It's contrived and pointless, and the woman doesn't even seem to experience any depth of emotion beyond "i'm sad that my friend stopped writing, oh no i have a brain tumor, but no worries this emotional epiphany will save the day!" It almost reads as a parody.
